page: Microsoft Azure D8ls_v7 is an x86_64 general-purpose virtual machine belonging to the low-memory Dlsv7 series, provisioned via Microsoft Hyper-V. The instance is powered by an Intel Xeon 6973P-C processor clocked at 4.2 GHz, configured with 8 vCPUs across 4 physical cores with multithreading enabled. The CPU includes an expansive 480 MB L3 cache, 2 MB of L2 cache per core, and hardware instruction support spanning AVX-512, AMX (tile and int8), and VAES. System memory is sized at 16.0 GB, providing a lean allocation of 2.0 GB per vCPU.

The instance does not include bundled local storage or discrete graphics processing units, relying entirely on network-attached storage with Premium Storage support. In benchmark testing, the Intel processor demonstrates strong performance in single-threaded data compression workloads, achieving 36.07 GB/sec in single-threaded gzip compression and 14.99 GB/sec in bzip3 decompression, alongside solid small-model LLM generation output at 266.79 tokens per second. General multi-core compute and memory bandwidth fall squarely in the mid-tier range, recording 85.56 GB/sec on uncached 256MB read tests and 15.64 million operations per second in Redis SET operations.

By constraining system memory to 2.0 GB per vCPU while maintaining dedicated high-frequency compute cores and AMX acceleration, the D8ls_v7 offers a cost-efficient resource footprint for CPU-heavy tasks that do not demand extensive memory buffers. The primary operational trade-off is the lack of local temporary NVMe storage and the lower memory-to-vCPU ratio. This profile makes the instance well suited for continuous integration and build pipelines, web serving clusters, batch compression utilities, microservices, and lightweight machine learning inference.

It features an Intel Xeon 6973P-C processor running at 4.2 GHz with 8 vCPUs across 4 physical cores, complemented by a substantial 480 MB L3 cache and hardware support for AVX-512 and AMX extensions. System memory is configured at 16.0 GB, establishing a 2.0 GB per vCPU ratio. The reduced memory ratio provides an efficient architecture for compute-bound operations that bypass heavy memory requirements, fitting workloads such as batch data processing, build servers, microservices, and web tier serving.
